title: Bruno Guimaraes Fails Mikel Arteta’s Challenge Against Newcastle—He Wasn’t Alone
subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Grey Whitebloom4:30 PM ESTBruno Guimarães had a mixed return to Newcastle. / Harvey Murphy/Danehouse/Getty ImagesNEWCASTLE — “I never felt so loved like the way I was at Newcastle,” Bruno Guimarães wistfully reflected after leaving the Magpies for Arsenal in a hotly contentious transfer over the summer. The Brazilian was taught the harsh lesson of how fickle love can be in this sport upon his return to the north east on Saturday.

The case of Guimarães is far more complicated than a straightforward betrayal, but it inspired a reception from the St James’ Park crowd befitting the reincarnation of Judas. As Guimarães stood over the ball waiting to take the opening kickoff, the hive of boos buzzed even louder than the instrumental rock blaring out of the stadium’s speaker system.

Arsenal’s $101 million recruit was relentlessly targeted throughout his 70 minutes on the pitch in a performance that was at its best when he was anonymous. But this reception was to be expected. “He has prepared emotionally,” Mikel Arteta warned pregame. It didn’t pay off.

That mental steeliness has been a feature of Arsenal’s entire season, with Arteta repeatedly stressing the importance of “emotional dominance.” Guimarães was not the only visitor who failed to match those demands in an unusually chaotic 2–2 draw for the Premier League champions.

Bruno Guimarães didn’t have a dream homecoming. / Stu Forster/Getty Images“I know that footballers are not gods,” Guimarães has admitted. “We are just people. We get nervous, just like anybody.” The nerves must have peaked before Saturday’s febrile reception from the city that remains a big part of his life.

This was a club captain who wholeheartedly embraced his home for four-and-a-half years, christening his son an honorary “Geordie” while he (half-)jokingly assumed the title of “the mayor of Newcastle.” Fans would constantly mob the club’s talismanic midfielder as he walked with his family through the winding streets, receiving countless selfie requests, bursts of praise and even some stern words from mothers. “Bruno, can you please change your hair?” he recalled being asked on more than one occasion. “My daughter only wants white hair now.”
Yet the nature of his summer exit, a move made in silence by the player to the backdrop of some very loud reports which made his desire to join Arsenal abundantly clear, rankled those on Tyneside.

Adam, a Newcastle season ticket holder with the club’s badge tattooed onto a calf exposed to the freezing cold conditions on the weekend, admitted that Guimarães “had to be booed” after a “sneaky” summer, just as a way of putting Arsenal off as much as punishment for the individual in question.

The initial impact was one of inhibition. Guimarães didn’t venture a vaguely adventurous pass across the opening 25 minutes, seemingly intent on limiting the boos by touching the ball as fleetingly as possible. That was his best spell in the match.

Arteta’s definition of “emotional dominance” is finding “the emotional state that the game requires and not something else.” There are times for the chest pumping roars which made Guimarães such a fan favorite at St James’ and the opposite is very much true. “If the game demands everybody to bring the temperature down,” Arteta explained, “we have to be able to do that.”

After easing his way in, Guimarães seemed to be emboldened for the rest of the first half, charging up the pitch with increasing frequency, lunging at one cross from Declan Rice which skewed narrowly wide. Arteta, however, noticeably berated his midfielder for straying out of position at one point, wary of those reins loosening too far. At least there was something Guimarães did to shout about. He simply vanished in the second half—along with the rest of the team.

Martin Ødegaard got swept along in the chaos. / David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesThe mental fortitude Arteta is striving for evaporated into the night sky with the hot air of his breath in second half.

David Raya’s injury within the opening minute of the second half completely deflated the visitors, who never seemed to shake out of the frost which formed while waiting for his two-minute medical treatment to end.

By the time that Raya eventually returned to his feet to punt the ball forward, the only Arsenal player to touch the ball with his feet before Tino Livramento’s equalizer was Martin Ødegaard, whose uncharacteristically wayward swipe squirmed through to present Newcastle with a golden opening.

A similarly sloppy slip from Eberechi Eze gave away the corner from which Malick Thiaw fired the hosts in front. The center back had an easy, unchallenged finish from close range as Gabriel, Raya and Joe Willock were knotted together on the goal line, a flurry of mismatching studs trying (and failing) to prod at the ball.
Arteta was seething with a thinly veiled fury after the final whistle.
“One thing is to give them belief, another thing is to give them a goal. We did both.”

During his 25 minutes on the pitch in the second half, Guimarães had just five touches of the ball, wilting under the weight of intensity from his emboldened former teammates. Ødegaard only had three touches while Arsenal were drowning.

Without those two central figures, the Gunners were bludgeoned into submission. Newcastle had scored twice, forced off Arsenal’s goalkeeper and went close to a third before the visitors even had a second-half shot. Newcastle manager Matthias Jaissle fairly described the league leaders as “shaking” in those latter 45 minutes.

However, Newcastle have their own emotional struggles. St James’ Park was an angry place outside of the Guimarães spotlight, giving in to frustrated groans at even the slightest provocation during a one-sided first half. The energy the turnaround inspired sent Newcastle a little too much on the front foot, leaving themselves bizarrely exposed while holding onto a 2–1 lead.
